818956e296.q: What time periods must be tracked separately when paying California drivers by the mile?
818956e296.a: When California's piece-rate requirements apply, nonproductive time such as pre-trip inspections, waiting to load, fueling, and paperwork must be separated out and paid distinctly. Qualified rest and recovery periods also require separate compensation calculations and wage statement entries. The key principle is that mileage pay doesn't satisfy the requirement to pay for all hours worked, particularly when the wheels aren't turning but the driver remains under employer control.

9221a21e05.q: What is the difference between an unpaid meal period and paid work time under California wage rules?
9221a21e05.a: A bona fide unpaid meal period requires the employee to be completely relieved of all duties. Federal guidance generally treats short rest breaks as paid work time. If a driver eats while monitoring loading, moving the truck, handling required calls, or filling out paperwork, that is not a qualifying unpaid meal period and must be paid as work time. A proper meal period that can be unpaid must be completely free of duties—if the employer contacts the driver once during a 30-minute meal period, it resets and the entire period becomes paid work time.

edc8042a15.q: How should detention policies be structured when customer agreements differ from driver payment obligations?
edc8042a15.a: A customer's detention billing arrangement (such as free time for the first two hours, then charging 50 to 75 dollars per hour) is separate from the driver's work-time payment obligations. Even if a customer agreement allows free loading time before billing begins, the driver must still be paid for all hours worked under California wage rules. The driver's duties and applicable wage rules determine payment; the customer's detention policy does not. This means a company must be prepared to pay the driver for all time, whether or not the customer is being billed for detention.

32cc1f9f88.q: Why does dividing total mileage earnings by work hours fail to prove California piece-rate wage compliance?
32cc1f9f88.a: While calculating an hourly average (for example, dividing 325 dollars in mileage earnings by 11 hours and 20 minutes of work time to get 28.68 dollars per hour) may show a reasonable-looking rate, it does not establish that all required separate compensation has been paid. California law requires that certain categories of time—such as nonproductive time and qualified rest periods—receive their own separate payment calculations and wage statement entries. An hourly average is a management illustration, not a compliance verification; companies must identify relevant time categories and calculate the required separate compensation for each…
32cc1f9f88.e: S2 E14 - How to Track Driver Hours When You Pay by the Mile
f: While calculating an hourly average (for example, dividing 325 dollars in mileage earnings by 11 hours and 20 minutes of work time to get 28.68 dollars per hour) may show a reasonable-looking rate, it does not establish that all required separate compensation has been paid. California law requires that certain categories of time—such as nonproductive time and qualified rest periods—receive their own separate payment calculations and wage statement entries. An hourly average is a management illustration, not a compliance verification; companies must identify relevant time categories and calculate the required separate compensation for each, not simply rely on total check division.
